title: Candy Corn Bag

drivers.name: Price increase to $4.08
drivers.evidence: Two prior weeks at $4.08 saw sales 13 and 3 units (vs baseline 10.1); noise-adjusted price effect estimate x0.80; consistent with demand elasticity.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 10.1. No events or promotions are scheduled. The price is raised 6.0% above regular ($3.85 → $4.08), which is a known demand deterrent. Past price hikes to $4.08 (2026-09-28, 2026-10-05) saw sales drop to 13 and 3 units respectively—both below baseline. The noise-adjusted effect of price increases is estimated at x0.80 (20% sales reduction). The classical uplift model ignores this, but historical price sensitivity is clear. No promotion or event drivers exist. The median multiplier is adjusted downward to 0.80, with downside spread widened slightly due to uncertainty in price elasticity.

brief:
PRODUCT: Candy Corn Bag | category Candy | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-30 to 2026-12-06 (8 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 4.08 (+6.0% vs regular price 3.85)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 10.1 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 25.9 | 10%-90%: 0.0 - 20.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-85% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
